paras: The lynching of William Beaver took place near Warren, Bradley County, Arkansas, on the night of August 10, 1890, when an armed mob took the young Black man from the county sheriff and hanged him. Beaver had been accused of attempting to assault Inez Abernathy, the daughter of the man he lived with, and a Black girl. An Arkansas City dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within days, many of them under headlines that endorsed the killing.

According to the Arkansas City dispatch, Beaver was about twenty years old and lived with a Mr. Abernathy near Warren. The dispatch said that on Friday morning, August 8, he attacked Abernathy's daughter Inez while she was gathering eggs in her father's lot, and that she fought him off and screamed until her mother came from the house. That evening, the same account said, he made a similar attempt on a Black girl near Mr. Sutton's plantation. Beaver was killed before any trial, and the accusations rest on the dispatch alone.

When news of the accusation spread on Friday night, a posse was organized to arrest Beaver. Sheriff Watson and a deputy captured him on Sunday evening a few miles from Warren and started for the jail with their prisoner. On the way they were met by "an armed mob of some eight or ten men," who took Beaver from Watson, locked the sheriff and his deputy in the jail, and hanged Beaver from a limb. The next morning his body was found hanging from a rope on the public square.
The coverage does not report an inquest, any arrests of mob members, or any statement from the sheriff after the lynching.

Two versions left Arkansas City on August 11: a short brief saying the sheriff had captured Beaver for an assault on "a young white lady," and a longer special that the Savannah Morning News credited to the Gazette. Morning papers from New York to Sacramento ran one or the other on August 12, often on page one. The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined it "A Colored Brute Lynched by a Mob" and called Beaver "the fiend," and the Wichita Daily Eagle put it under "Law's Delay Avoided." Other headlines were "Judge Lynch Sealed His Fate," "Judge Lynch Presided" and "Beaver's Case Soon Settled," while The Sun and the Indianapolis Journal used plainer ones.

Over the next ten days the story shrank to a sentence in weekly news-summary columns. In rewriting, some papers moved the lynching to "Arkansas City, Neb." or "Arkansas City, Kan.," and one ran it under the headline "Negro Lynched in Nebraska." A "Sins and Sinners" paragraph that ran in Minnesota and Dakota weeklies through August 23 added that the officers "were locked in the jail until the lynching was over." No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

Accounts differ on details. The August 12 dispatch named the young woman Miss Inez Abernathy, while an August 13 version called her "Mrs. Lucy Abernathy." That version also said Beaver was arrested after the second attack and taken from the sheriff "later in the evening," and a Delaware brief put the mob's action on Monday night. The fuller Arkansas City dispatch, the earliest and most detailed account, gives a Sunday-evening capture, with the body found the next morning.

accounts.label: Arkansas City special (full dispatch)
accounts.gist: Beaver attacked Inez Abernathy Friday morning and a Black girl that evening, was captured Sunday by Sheriff Watson, and was taken by an armed mob of eight or ten men who locked up the officers and hanged him; the body was found on the public square the next morning.

accounts.label: Short Arkansas City brief
accounts.gist: The sheriff captured Beaver 'last night' for an assault on 'a young white lady' and a mob met him on the way to jail and hanged the prisoner to a tree.

accounts.label: Aug. 13 variant
accounts.gist: Beaver attacked 'Mrs. Lucy Abernathy', then a colored girl, was arrested, and a crowd took him from the sheriff and hanged him to a tree, in one version 'later in the evening'.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined 'A Colored Brute Lynched by a Mob' and called Beaver 'the fiend' and 'the would-be rapist'.
The Wichita Daily Eagle headlined 'Law's Delay Avoided. A Would-be Rapist Hanged in a Public Square.'
The Savannah Morning News and Rock Island Argus used 'Judge Lynch Sealed His Fate' and 'Beaver's Case Soon Settled'.
The Sun and Indianapolis Journal ran the dispatch with factual headlines ('Lynched a Negro', 'Hanged in the Public Square'), and many weeklies cut it to one line in news-brief columns.

conflicts.note: Arkansas City was the dateline; the full dispatch places the events near Warren and the Nebraska and Kansas versions are rewrite errors.
